title: Singleton and Builder
idea: Singleton guarantees a class has exactly one instance with one access point. Builder assembles a complex, immutable object step by step, then validates it once in `build()`.
points: A Singleton hides its constructor and hands out one shared instance.
The holder idiom and the `enum` form are thread-safe without explicit locking.
A Builder collects optional values in a mutable helper, then creates the object.
`build()` checks the rules once, so every built object starts valid.

hero.caption: Singleton controls how many objects exist; Builder controls how one object is assembled.

code.title: Singleton
code.caption: Two common Java singletons: a lazy holder class and a one-constant `enum`.

walk.text: A `private` constructor stops any other class from calling `new`.
The nested holder loads on first use; the JVM creates the instance once.
`get` is the single access point. No `synchronized` is needed here.
Shared mutable state still needs guarding, so `next` is `synchronized`.
A one-constant `enum` is also a singleton. Unlike the holder, reflection and deserialization cannot copy it.
Both references point at one object, so the counter is shared.

code.title: Builder
code.caption: Named steps replace a long constructor. `build()` refuses an email without a subject.

walk.text: The product has only `private final` fields: immutable once built.
Its constructor is `private` and copies from the builder, including a safe list copy.
A static entry point takes the required field up front.
The builder holds draft values; each setter returns `this` to allow chaining.
`build()` validates, then creates the product in one step.
`main` builds one valid email and sees a missing subject refused.

pitfalls: Do not use a Singleton as a hidden global; pass dependencies through constructors instead.
Avoid lazy `if (instance == null)` without locking; two threads can create two instances.
Validate in `build()`, not in setters, so rules that span fields hold.

quiz.q: What is the second line `SingletonDemo` prints?
quiz.why: `a` and `b` are the same `Sequence`, so all three `next()` calls bump one shared counter: 1, then 2, then 3.

takeaway: Singleton limits how many exist; Builder makes one valid object readably.
